did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with the heading “A Song of Ascents” and the cry “Out of the depths.” The phrase can describe deep distress, yet from that place the psalmist calls out to the Lord rather than remaining in despair.
The psalmist asks not only for the Lord to hear, but for His ears to be “attentive to the sound of his pleas”—an expression emphasizing careful attention to prayer and supplication.
The question “If You, Lord, kept a record of sins, Lord, who could stand?” highlights human weakness: if every sin were counted and held against us, no one could withstand judgment.

The verse “But with You there is forgiveness” places forgiveness at the center of hope. As the rest of the verse suggests, forgiveness does not eliminate the fear of the Lord; rather, it makes that reverence possible.

This verse contains several expressions of waiting: “I wait,” “my soul waits,” and “I put my hope.” The repetition emphasizes that waiting for the Lord is a deep desire of the heart, directed also toward His word.

The psalmist compares his soul’s longing for the Lord to watchmen waiting for the morning. The repetition of “watchmen waiting for the morning” strengthens the sense of alert and persistent expectation.

In the first half of the chapter, the psalmist speaks mainly in the first person, but here he addresses all Israel: “O Israel, hope in the Lord.” In this way, personal hope becomes the hope of the entire people.

The reason Israel is called to hope is that “with the Lord is unfailing love, and with Him is abundant redemption.” The verse presents steadfast love and redemption as qualities or powers found in the Lord.

The chapter concludes by moving from hope to promise: the Lord “will redeem Israel from all its sins.” Redemption is therefore described not only as deliverance from trouble, but also as salvation from sin.
